titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§267–270: The fall of the Tangut, Ögödei’s accession and the western campaigns
part: §§267–270 — The fall of the Tangut, Ögödei’s accession and the western campaigns
about: Chinggis takes Dörmegei and receives Burqan’s homage, but is revolted by it; he has the Tangut ruler put to death, shares out the spoils, and decrees that the Tangut be wiped out. In the Pig year he goes up to Heaven. Two years on, the princes gather at Ködö’e-Aral and raise Ögödei Qan, and Cha’adai and Tolui hand over the guard and the central people. Ögödei sends armies west against Sultan Qaliba and, under Sübegetei, as far as the Adil and Jajaq, appoints Batu and Güyük as elders of the princes, and rules that each prince send his eldest son on campaign. A note on the text: the Mongol is a Ming Chinese-character transcription, and the glosses in square brackets are the Ming glossators’ own; where the English departs from them or is unsure, the note says so.

sentences.t: Čiṅgis Qaγan Časutu-ača ködölžü Uraγai balaγasu baγ̇užu
sentences.l: Chinggis Qaγan, from Časutu setting out, Uraγai town descending,
sentences.i: Chinggis Qahan set out from Časutu and halted at the town of Uraqai,
sentences.n: Čiṅgis Qaγan Časutu-ača ködölžü begins a chain of converbs (-žü / -žu, “-ing”): setting out … halting … and the finite verb only comes at the end of the next unit’s sentence. Časutu has the Ming gloss 山名 處, “mountain name, from”; baγ̇užu is “descending”, which the Ming (下) and the house rendering take as “camping, halting”.

sentences.t: Uraγai balaγasun-ača ködölžü Dörmegei balaγasu ebden büküi-dür

sentences.n: Balaγasun-ača is “from the town” (the ablative -ača, Ming 處). Ebden is the converb of ebde- “break”, and büküi-dür is bü- “to be” + the participle -küi + the dative-locative, “at the being”, that is “while / when it was so” (Ming 有 時). Dörmegei is glossed 靈州, a Chinese city name, so a Tangut town.

sentences.t: Burqan Čiṅgis Qaγan-(n)a aγ̇ulžara irebe.
sentences.l: Burqan to Chinggis Qaγan homage-to-pay came.
sentences.i: Burqan came to pay homage to Chinggis Qahan.
sentences.n: Here the Ming gloss for Burqan is 人名, “a man’s name”, not “mountain”, so this is the Tangut ruler, as in §265. Aγ̇ulžara is the purposive converb, “in order to have an audience” (Ming 拜見), and Qaγan-(n)a is the dative with the Ming 行. Irebe “came” closes the sentence.

sentences.i: There, as Burqan paid homage, the gifts began with gold Buddhas (?), then gold and silver cups and vessels,
sentences.n: Aγ̇ulžarun is “when paying homage”. Sümes is the Ming 佛每, “Buddhas” in the plural; the Mongol word is süme “temple”, so “images” would be a fair guess, and I mark it uncertain. The Mongol states no verb for the gifts; “the gifts” is my supply to carry the list, and teriġülen is “heading, beginning with”.

sentences.t: jesün jesüd muγ̇ud ökid jesün jesüd aγtas temeġed jesün jesüd eldeb(i)-jer jesün jesüd žisüležü
sentences.l: nine nines of boys, girls, nine nines of geldings, camels, nine nines with every kind, arranged by kind,
sentences.i: nine times nine boys and girls, nine times nine geldings and camels, and nine times nine of every other kind, all arranged by kind,
sentences.n: Jesün jesüd is “nine, nines”, the ritual ninefold of Mongol gift-giving; the Ming marks the plural with (每). Muγ̇ud is glossed 兒(每), “boys”, but its Han (訥…) points to a nu- beginning, so the reading is uncertain. Eldeb(i)-jer (Ming 諸般 敎, “of all kinds”) has an ending shaped like an instrumental, and žisüležü is žisü “colour, kind” made into a verb (Ming 色樣着, “in kinds”); both are tentative.

sentences.t: aγ̇ulžaqui-dur Burqan-i egüden büteġüj-e aγ̇ulžaγ̇ulba.
sentences.l: homage-paying-at, Burqan-(object) door in-the-dark(?) had-pay-homage.
sentences.i: and at the homage he had Burqan do his obeisance at the door, in the dark.
sentences.n: Aγ̇ulžaγ̇ulba is the causative, “had (him) pay homage”, with Burqan-i as object; the subject is not named, and “he” is Chinggis by the sense. Büteġüj-e is the hard word: the Ming 暗 行 gives “in the dark”, and büteġü- elsewhere is “complete” (§267 büteġebe), but a büteġü meaning “shut” is possible, so “at the closed door” may be intended. I follow the Ming and say so.

sentences.t: Tere aγ̇ulžaqui- dur Čiṅgis Qaγan dotora dura bulγaba.
sentences.l: That homage-paying at, Chinggis Qaγan within heart-evil stirred.
sentences.i: At that homage Chinggis Qahan felt revulsion within him.
sentences.n: The three Ming glosses read together are 內 … 惡 … 心了, “within … evil … hearted”, which in Chinese runs together as 惡心, “to feel sick, to be disgusted”. So bulγaba, otherwise “to fight”, here means “was stirred, was turned”; I translate by the Ming’s sense. The text does not say why he was revolted.

sentences.t: "Iluqu-Burqan-a Šidurqu nere ögčü Iluqu-Burqan Šidurqu-ji iregdežü tende Čiṅgis Qaγan Iluqu-ji nögčijefkün keġen
sentences.l: "To Iluqu-Burqan Šidurqu name giving, Iluqu-Burqan Šidurqu-(object) being-come-to, there Chinggis Qaγan Iluqu-(object) let-him-pass-away saying,
sentences.i: “Having given Iluqu-Burqan the name Shidurqu, and Iluqu-Burqan Shidurqu having been come to, Chinggis Qahan said there, ‘Let Iluqu be put to death,’ and said,
sentences.n: The quotation opens here and runs to nögčiġetügei in the unit after next. It speaks of Chinggis in the third person, which is odd inside his own decree, and the clause iregdežü (the passive of ire- “come”, Ming 被來着, “being come”) with Šidurqu-ji in the accusative does not parse cleanly, so the middle of this unit is my best reading, not a sure one. Nögčijefkün is printed with an f, probably a slip for -kün; the Ming 敎過去者 means “let (him) be made to pass away”, a euphemism, so “put to death”. Two keġen “saying” stand in the decree; I give them as “said”.

sentences.n: The closing quotation mark is Shiratori’s, after nögčiġetügei, the third-person optative “let him …” (-tügei, Ming 者). Γardažu “laying a hand on” (Ming 下手着) is the converb of γarda-, from γar “hand”. Čerbi is a title whose meaning is not known (house: “cherbi”, not “chamberlain”). Žarliγ bolba is the finite “made a decree”.

sentences.t: Tende Tolun Čerbi Iluqu-ji γardažu büteġebe keġen öčiġešü
sentences.l: There Tolun Čerbi Iluqu-(object) hand-laying completed saying, when-reported,
sentences.i: When Tolun the cherbi reported that he had laid hands on Iluqu there and finished him,
sentences.n: Büteġebe is büteġe- + the past -be; the Ming 完備 is “complete, make whole”, which I take as “finished the matter, dispatched him”. Keġen “saying” is the report; öčiġešü is the conditional converb, “if / when (he) reported”, and the Ming 奏呵 uses 奏 for speaking up to a superior. The whole is a subordinate “when”, resolved in the next unit.

sentences.t: "Taṅγ̇ud irgen-dür üge olulčan aisuqui-dur
sentences.l: "Tangut people-to word dispute(?) coming-at-the-time,
sentences.i: “When I came to the Tangut people to call them to account for their words,
sentences.n: The quotation opens again and, unlike the first, Shiratori prints no closing mark; I close it in `i` after “vessels”, at the end of Tolun’s share. Irgen-dür “to the people” has the Ming 行, and aisuqui-dur is aisu- “come” + the participle -qui + the dative, “at the coming”. Olulčan is glossed 折證, “to confront, adjudicate”; the Mongol word is not clear to me, so “to call them to account” is a guess from the Ming. The speaker is Chinggis; “I” is not in the Mongol.

sentences.n: Žaγ̇ura is “in the middle, on the way” (Ming 路間). Anatuγai is the optative of a stem I read from the Ming 敎痊疴者, “let it be healed”; marija is “flesh, body”.

sentences.t: Nökör küġün-ü qoron üge-dür irežü
sentences.l: Companion man’s poison word-in coming,
sentences.i: Having come to hear a companion’s poisonous words,
sentences.n: Nökör is “companion” and küġün-ü the genitive of “man”; qoron is the Ming 毒 “poison”, so this is the poisoned or slanderous word of a fellow. I do not know whose speech this is — it is not said — and “having come to hear” is a loose rendering of üge-dür irežü, literally “having come to the word”.

sentences.t: müṅke teṅgeri-de küčü nemegdežü γar-tur(i)-jan oroγ̇ulžu öši-jen abuγ̇ai-že bida.

sentences.i: with strength added to us by Eternal Heaven, we brought him into our own hands and took our own revenge.
sentences.n: Teṅgeri-de is the dative-locative naming the doer of a passive (Ming 天 行, “by Heaven”); nemegdežü is neme- “add” + passive + converb. Γar-tur(i)-jan is “in one’s own hand” (reflexive -(i)jan; the (i) is Shiratori’s), and bida is “we” (inclusive, Ming 咱). “Him” is my supply: the Mongol does not say whom they brought into their hands.

sentences.i: and, while you eat your food, saying ‘Let there be no muquli musquli,’ put them to death, wipe them out, and keep saying so, all of you,”
sentences.n: Ideġe ideküi žaγ̇ura is “while the food is eaten” (Ming 茶飯 喫的 間), so the command is to say the curse at every meal. Üküġülün “making die” and ečidgen “bringing to an end” (Ming 敎絕) are converbs, and kelelen “speaking”. Adqun has the Ming 您, “you (plural)”: I take -dqun as one ending of the second-person plural command, “you shall”. Both the verb sense and the reading are tentative.

sentences.i: “And of those who came out of the centre, let Güyük be their elder,” he said, and issued a decree.
sentences.n: Γol-ača γaruγsad-i is “from the centre, those who went out” (Ming 在內處 出了的每 行), the other division of the princes. Same ending as the unit before: keġen žarliγ bolba. Here Shiratori prints the opening and closing marks both.

morph.gloss: to go out (verb) [出了的每 行]
past participle, plural: those who …ed (back-vowel form)
Güyük, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
optative: let him … (third person, back-vowel form)

sentences.t: Ede ajalaqun-i ulus modekün köġüd köġüd-ü-ġen kü jeke köġü ajalaγ̇ultuγai.
sentences.l: These campaigners-(object) people ruling princes, their-own-sons indeed great son let-them-have-campaign.
sentences.i: “As for these who go on campaign: let the princes who govern the realm have their own sons campaign, the eldest son.
sentences.n: Shiratori prints no opening mark for this decree, so the opening quotation mark in `i` is mine; the closing mark is at ajalaγ̇ultuγai in §270’s unit 414–421. Ajalaγ̇ultuγai is “let (him) cause to campaign”, and modekün is mede- “know, manage” + -kün, printed with o (Ming 管的每). Köġüd-ü-ġen is “their own sons” (a linking -ü- before the reflexive after the plural). Jeke köġü is “great son”, the eldest; kü is the particle “indeed”. My reading of the accusative ajalaqun-i is a guess.

morph.gloss: to go on campaign (verb) [征進的每 行]
to know, to manage, rule (printed modekün with o; verb) [管的每]
to go on campaign (verb) [敎征進者︀]

sentences.t: Ulus ba ülü modekün köġüd
sentences.l: People also not ruling princes,
sentences.i: And the princes who do not govern the realm,
sentences.n: Ba is “also, and” (Ming 也); ülü modekün is “not ruling”, the negative of the unit before.

morph.gloss: to know, to manage, rule (printed modekün with o; verb) [管的每]

sentences.t: tümed-ün miṅγad-un žaγ̇ud-un harbad-un nojad olon küġün ken ber böġesü
sentences.l: ten-thousands’, thousands’, hundreds’, tens’ lords, many men whoever even-if-there-be,
sentences.i: the commanders of ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds and tens, and any other man of the many, whoever he may be,
sentences.n: Four genitive plurals in a row (tümed-ün miṅγad-un žaγ̇ud-un harbad-un, Ming 萬每的 … 十每的) qualify nojad “lords”. Ken ber böġesü is “whoever, even if (it) be”, the “if it be” conditional böġesü after ber “even”.

sentences.t: köġüd-ü-ġen aqa-ji ajalaγ̇ultuγai.
sentences.l: their-own-sons eldest-(object) let-them-have-campaign.
sentences.i: each is to have his own eldest son campaign.
sentences.n: Aqa-ji is “the elder (object)” (Ming 長 行), used of the eldest son; köġüd-ü-ġen as before.

morph.gloss: accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
to go on campaign (verb) [敎征進者︀]

sentences.t: Ökid küriged mün josu-γ̇ar köġüd-ü-ġen kü aqa-ji ajalaγ̇ultuγai"
sentences.l: Daughters, sons-in-law just rule-by, their-own-sons indeed eldest-(object) let-them-have-campaign"
sentences.i: The daughters and sons-in-law, by the same rule, are to have their own eldest sons campaign.”
sentences.n: Ökid küriged is “the daughters, the sons-in-law” (Ming 女每 婿每); mün josu-γ̇ar is “by the very same rule”. Shiratori’s closing mark comes after the last ajalaγ̇ultuγai, closing the decree begun at Ede ajalaqun-i.

morph.gloss: custom, proper way, rule (noun) [理 依着]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
to go on campaign (verb) [敎征進者︀]

sentences.t: keġen žarliγ boluγ̇ad
sentences.l: saying decree having-made,
sentences.i: So he said, and when the decree was made,
sentences.n: Boluγ̇ad is bol- + a linking -u- + the converb -γ̇ad, “having made”, the back-vowel form (Ming 做了). It leads straight into the next sentence.

morph.gloss: to become, to be made (verb) [做了]

sentences.t: basa Ögödei Qaγan ügülerün:
sentences.l: Again Ögödei Qaγan speaking:
sentences.i: Ögödei Qahan spoke again:
sentences.n: Basa is “again”; ügülerün is ügüle- “speak” + the converb of time -rün, “when speaking”, as for žarliγ bolurun. Shiratori’s colon marks the speech that follows.

morph.gloss: Ögödei, a man's name (personal name) [人名]

sentences.t: "Ene ba köġüd-ün aqa-ji ajalaγ̇ulqu josun Čaγ̇adai aqa-ača bolžuγ̇u-že.
sentences.l: "This also sons’ eldest-(object) to-make-campaign custom, Cha’adai elder-brother-from has-been-made.
sentences.i: “And this custom too, of making the eldest of the sons campaign, came from my elder brother Cha’adai.
sentences.n: Ene ba is “this also” (Ming 這 也). Aqa-ji is “the eldest (object)”, and ajalaγ̇ulqu josun is “the custom of making (them) campaign” (the participle -qu before josun “custom, rule”, Ming 理). Aqa-ača is the ablative “from the elder brother”; bolžuγ̇u-že is “has been made, indeed” (past -žuγ̇u + -že). “My” is mine; Ögödei speaks.

morph.gloss: accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
to go on campaign (verb) [敎出征的]

sentences.t: Čaγ̇adai aqa ügüležü irerün Sübeġetei-jin
sentences.l: Cha’adai elder-brother speaking when-coming,
sentences.i: My elder brother Cha’adai, speaking as he came, said:
sentences.n: I take Ögödei still to be speaking, and the next stretch to be Cha’adai’s own words, reported inside his: ügüležü is “speaking” (Ming 說着), irerün “as he comes” (Ming 來的). The inner quotation has no marks in Shiratori; I add single quotes in `i`.

morph.gloss: Cha'adai, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
Sübegetei, a man's name (personal name) [人名的]

sentences.t: gežige köġüd-ü-ġen aqa Buri-ji ajalaγ̇ulumu.
sentences.l: Sübegetei’s reserve, his-own-sons’ eldest Büri-(object) makes-campaign.
sentences.i: ‘As the reserve of Sübegetei I am sending Büri, the eldest of my sons, on campaign.
sentences.n: Ajalaγ̇ulumu is ajala- + the causative -γ̇ul- + -umu, a present-tense ending (Ming 敎征進有, “causes to campaign”); I read it as present with “I”, since the reflexive köġüd-ü-ġen “his own sons” is Cha’adai’s. The person is not marked in the Mongol, so this is my reading.

morph.gloss: Büri, a man's name (personal name) [人名 行]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
to go on campaign (verb) [敎征進有]

sentences.t: Köġüd-ün aqa ajalaγ̇asu čerig arbin γarqu čerig olon boluγ̇asu
sentences.l: Sons’ eldest if-campaigns, army broad going-out, army many if-it-becomes,
sentences.i: When the eldest of the sons campaigns, and the army that goes out is broad, and the army is many,
sentences.n: Köġüd-ün aqa is “the eldest of the sons”. Ajalaγ̇asu and boluγ̇asu are the conditional converbs, “if / when” (Ming 呵). Arbin is “wide, broad” (Ming 寬廣), čerig “army”, γarqu the participle “that goes out”.

sentences.t: čirai deġere küčütej-e jabuju.
sentences.l: face above, strength-having goes-about.
sentences.i: he goes about with head high and with strength.
sentences.n: Čirai deġere is “face above” (Ming 顏色 高), a high countenance, I take as pride or confidence. Küčütej-e is küčü “strength” + the possessive -tei + the dative-locative, “with strength”. Jabuju is the converb jabuža written with j, but standing as the finite verb (Ming 行有), “goes about”, which is uncertain.

morph.gloss: converb -žu written with j, standing here as a finite 'is going about' (uncertain)

sentences.t: Činadu daisun küġün olon qarin bi.
sentences.l: Beyond enemy men many nations there-are.
sentences.i: Beyond them are enemies, many men and many peoples.
sentences.n: Činadu is “the far side, beyond” (Ming 那廂); daisun is “enemy”, and qarin has the Ming 邦, “nation, state”, which the house takes as tentative “nation”. Bi is “there are” (Ming 有).

morph.gloss: nation, people (noun; Ming 邦 'nation', tentative) [邦]
to be, there is (verb; short form) [有]

sentences.t: Tere üžeġür-e kečeġün irgen tede kiliṅlaγ̇asu öġer-ün mese-dür(i)-jen ükükün.
sentences.l: That tip-at hard people, they if-enraged, own weapons-on those-who-die.
sentences.i: At that far edge there is a stubborn people, and when they are enraged they die on their own weapons.
sentences.n: Üžeġür-e is “at the tip, extremity” (Ming 梢頭 行), and kečeġün the Ming 剛硬, “hard, unyielding”. Kiliṅlaγ̇asu is “if / when enraged” (Ming 怒了呵), and mese-dür(i)-jen ükükün is “those who die on their own weapons” (Ming 器械 裏自的行 死的每), a people who fight to the death.

morph.gloss: hard, stubborn, unyielding (read from the Ming 剛硬) (adjective) [剛硬]
to be enraged, to be angry (stem inferred from the Ming 怒) (verb) [怒了呵]
reflexive-possessive: one's own (front-vowel form; the (i) is Shiratori's)

sentences.t: Irgen tede meses qurčatan keġegdemüi" keġežü irežüġüi.
sentences.l: People those weapons sharp-having is-called" saying came.
sentences.i: Those people are called the sharp-weaponed.’” So saying, he came.
sentences.n: Shiratori’s closing mark comes after keġegdemüi, “is called” (keġe- “say” + the passive -gde- + the present -müi, Ming 被說有). Qurčatan is a stem I read from the Ming 鋒利, “sharp”, + the plural-possessive -tan, “those having sharpness”. Keġežü irežüġüi is “saying, came”; the subject is not named, and I take it as Cha’adai arriving with the words.

morph.gloss: sharpness, a sharp edge (stem inferred from the Ming 鋒利) (noun) [鋒利有的(每)]

sentences.t: Ögödei Qaγan ügülerün:
sentences.l: Ögödei Qaγan speaking:
sentences.i: Ögödei Qahan said:
sentences.n: Ögödei speaks a second time; the formula is the same as at the head of his first speech, ügülerün with its colon.

morph.gloss: Ögödei, a man's name (personal name) [人名]

sentences.t: "Tere üge-dür bidan-u ber Čaγ̇adai aqa-jin kičijeṅgü küčü-ġer köġüd-ün aqa-ji γarγaja keġen
sentences.l: "That word-in us-of-also Cha’adai elder-brother’s careful strength-by, sons’ eldest-(object) let-us-send-out saying,
sentences.i: “By that word, and by the careful strength of Cha’adai, our elder brother, saying, ‘Let us send out the eldest of the sons,’
sentences.n: Tere üge-dür is “in that word” (Ming 言語 裏); bidan-u is “of us” (inclusive, Ming 咱的), with ber “also”. Kičijeṅgü is “careful, circumspect” (Ming 謹愼的), küčü-ġer “by strength”, and γarγaja is γar- “go out” + the causative -γa- + the hortative -ja, “let us send out” (Ming 敎出去咱). The inner single quotes are mine; Shiratori marks only the opening of the whole.

morph.gloss: we, us (inclusive pronoun; stem bidan-) [咱的]
Cha'adai, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
careful, diligent (read from the Ming 謹愼) (adjective) [謹︀愼的]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)

sentences.t: žüg žüg tuṅqaγ̇ažu
sentences.l: each direction each direction proclaiming,
sentences.i: we proclaimed it in every direction,
sentences.n: Žüg žüg is “each quarter, each quarter” (Ming 各處 各處), tuṅqaγ̇ažu “proclaiming” (Ming 宣布着). “We” is mine: the converb carries no person.

sentences.t: Batu, Büri, Güjüg, Münke teriġüten köġüd-i ajalaγ̇ulqui josun eimü bi-že."
sentences.l: Batu, Büri, Güyük, Müngke and-the-rest sons-(object) of-making-campaign custom thus it-is-indeed."
sentences.i: and such is the custom by which Batu, Büri, Güyük, Müngke and the other princes are made to campaign.”
sentences.n: Ajalaγ̇ulqui josun is “the custom of making (them) campaign” (Ming 敎征進的 理), the participle -qui before josun; köġüd-i is “the sons (object)”, with the names in apposition and teriġüten “and the rest”. Eimü bi-že is “it is thus, indeed” (Ming 這般 有也者). Shiratori’s closing quotation mark is at the end of this last word, closing Ögödei’s speech.
